## Today

1. Fit a network on Friday's churn table, properly — validation set, `size`, `decay`
2. Put it in the table next to logistic regression, the forest and the boosting
3. Watch it lose, and understand why
4. See what *deep* learning is, in one slide, and where it wins instead
5. Leave with a rule you can use on Monday

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} Fit one properly {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Step 1 — the same rows as last week

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-3|5-7|9"}
library(tidyverse); library(nnet); library(ranger); library(xgboost); library(here)
churn <- read_csv(here("data", "churn.csv")) |> select(-id) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), factor), y = churn == "yes")

set.seed(1)
tr  <- sample(nrow(churn), 4900)          # 70%, as in lecture 17
val <- sample(tr, 900)                    # carve a validation set out of training
trn <- setdiff(tr, val)

X <- model.matrix(y ~ . - churn - 1, churn) |> scale()   # dummies, then scale — networks need both
```

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
Three sets, not two. **Training** fits the weights, **validation** chooses `size` and `decay`, **test** is touched once, at the end, to report. Choose hyperparameters on the test set and your reported accuracy is fiction.
:::

## Step 2 — a grid, and the validation curve

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|4-9|11"}
grid <- expand_grid(size = c(1, 3, 5, 10, 20), decay = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1))
logloss <- function(p, y) -mean(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))

grid$val <- pmap_dbl(grid, function(size, decay) {
  set.seed(7)
  f <- nnet(X[trn, ], churn$y[trn], size = size, decay = decay, maxit = 300, trace = FALSE)
  p <- pmin(pmax(predict(f, X[val, ]), 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6)
  logloss(p, churn$y[val])
})

ggplot(grid, aes(size, val, colour = factor(decay))) + geom_line() + geom_point()
```

Read the plot before the next slide. Where is the minimum? What happens at `size = 20, decay = 0`? That is slide 17 of Monday, drawn by you.

## Step 3 — refit on all of training, score the test once

```{.r code-line-numbers="1|3-4|6"}
best <- grid[which.min(grid$val), ]                    # typically size 3–5, decay 0.01

set.seed(7)
nn <- nnet(X[tr, ], churn$y[tr], size = best$size, decay = best$decay, maxit = 500, trace = FALSE)

p_nn <- predict(nn, X[-tr, ])
```

Add logistic, forest and boosting **on the same `-tr` rows**, from last week's script. Then:

| Model | Accuracy | AUC | Log-loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| Logistic | | | |
| Pruned tree | | | |
| Random forest | | | |
| Gradient boosting | | | |
| Neural network | | | |

Fill it in. Then look at it for a while.

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} What you will see {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## The network loses. Here is why.

On a table of a few thousand customers with twenty columns, the order is almost always: **boosting ≥ forest > network ≈ logistic > tree**.

- Tabular data has *structure a tree can use*: thresholds, interactions between a few columns. Trees find them in one split. A network has to *discover* them through smooth functions of scaled dummies.
- With 5 000 rows, a network cannot learn much that a forest does not already know. It **can** learn the noise, and it needs your validation set to stop it.
- The network's advantage — arbitrary smooth nonlinearity — is not the shape of the signal here

::: {.callout-note}
This is not a defect of networks. It is a mismatch between the tool and the data. The same network on 50 000 images would win by a mile.
:::

## When the residuals tell you to reach for one

From Monday: the network with identity activation *is* OLS. So when does the nonlinearity earn its place?

- Fit the linear model. Plot predicted vs observed. **If the residuals curve**, the relationship is nonlinear.
- Option 1: transform the response, refit the regression, keep interpretability
- Option 2: assume the nonlinearity is real and complex → a network with nonlinear activations

Try option 1 first. It costs a minute and, more often than not, the curve was a log.

## [Section 3]{.section-kicker} Deep learning, in one slide {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## What "deep" means, and what it costs

MNIST: 28 × 28 pixel images of handwritten digits, 10 classes. A network: 784 → 1024 → 1024 → 2048 → 10.

$$
784\!\times\!1024 + 1024\!\times\!1024 + 1024\!\times\!2048 + 2048\!\times\!10 \;\approx\; \mathbf{4\ million\ weights}
$$

- *Deep*: more than one hidden layer. That is the whole definition.
- Four million weights, sixty thousand images: it **will** overfit without **dropout** — randomly switching off neurons during training, an ensemble of sub-networks — and weight decay
- The two architectures you will hear named: **CNNs** for images (convolution: local, shared filters — a 3×3 edge detector reused across the whole picture) and **RNNs** for sequences (the same weights applied at every time step — an autoregressive model with a memory)

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
None of these apply to a customer table. They win where the data have *spatial or sequential structure* the architecture can exploit: images, text, audio, sensor streams. On rows and columns, use last week's tools.
:::

## The one connection worth keeping

An **autoencoder** is a network trained to reproduce its own input through a narrow hidden layer: $p$ inputs → $q < p$ neurons → $p$ outputs, loss = reconstruction error.

- With **linear** activations, it converges to **PCA**. Exactly. The $q$ hidden neurons span the first $q$ components.
- With nonlinear activations it is a PCA that can bend — compression that follows curved structure

Lecture 14's last slide, closed. Unsupervised learning and neural networks are the same subject seen from two sides.

## [Section 4]{.section-kicker} The rule {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Which model, on Monday morning

| Your data are… | Start with | Consider a network when… |
|---|---|---|
| A table, < 100k rows | logistic → forest → boosting | never, unless residuals curve and transformations fail |
| A table, millions of rows, hundreds of columns | boosting | a well-tuned MLP is competitive; test it |
| Images, audio, free text, long sequences | a pretrained deep network | always — nothing else works |
| Anything where you must **explain** the decision | tree, logistic, GAM | only with lecture 20's tools, and a lawyer |

The honest version of every AI vendor pitch you will ever hear fits in this table.

## Deliverable

Ungraded, but bring it Wednesday:

- The five-model table, filled, on the test rows
- Your validation plot for the network, with the chosen `size` and `decay` marked
- One paragraph: *which model would you deploy for this company, and what would you tell the CFO about the one you did not choose?*

## The question is never "can a neural network do this?" It can. The question is whether anything simpler could — and it usually can.  {.statement}
